analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $17 and ends lower wages for tipped, teen, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The Raise the Wage Act of 2023, backed by 172 of 216 House Democrats, was referred to committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour in steps to $9.50, $11, $12.50, $14, $15.50, and finally $17, then adjust it automatically each year with the growth in the median wage. It would phase out the lower minimum wage for tipped workers, the reduced wage for newly hired teenagers, and the subminimum wage that lets employers pay workers with disabilities under special certificates. It took effect three months after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are paid at or near the federal minimum, including millions in food service, retail, and care work. Tipped workers, who in most states can be paid as little as $2.13 an hour in cash by their employers, would eventually get the full minimum wage with the right to keep their tips. Newly hired teenagers and workers with disabilities currently paid under special certificates would be moved onto the standard wage over time.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $9.50 on the effective date, then in annual steps to $11, $12.50, $14, $15.50, and $17, and after that indexes it to the growth in the median hourly wage so it never falls behind again.

Phases out the separate lower cash wage for tipped employees, lifting it in steps to $17 before the full standard minimum wage applies, and gives every employee the explicit right to keep their own tips.

Raises the subminimum wage for workers with disabilities in steps to the full minimum wage, bars any new special certificates, and sunsets the program entirely, while directing the Labor Secretary to help employers comply and to connect affected workers to competitive employment.
Raises the reduced wage for newly hired workers under 20 from $4.25 to $6.00 and then phases that exception out entirely.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that employ workers at or near the minimum wage — restaurants, retail stores, hotels, care providers, and other low-wage employers — would face higher payroll costs, with the steepest increases in states that still use the $7.25 federal floor or the tipped and subminimum exceptions. Some of that cost would be passed to consumers through prices, and employers of sheltered workshop workers would lose a wage structure they had relied on.

drawbacks.text: The bill directly raises the cost of employing minimum-wage and tipped labor, which falls hardest on small restaurants and other low-margin employers, particularly in states where the federal $7.25 wage is still the standard.

Eliminating the tipped-employee cash wage exception and the subminimum wage for workers with disabilities removes wage structures many employers in those industries have relied on, and some employers argue this reduces hiring or training opportunities for teenagers and workers with disabilities.

Opponents of federal minimum wage increases generally argue that the increases lead to some job losses or reduced hours for the lowest-paid workers, and that a single national wage ignores large differences in local living costs; this bill did not address those objections, for example with regional or small-business carve-outs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is substantial and well-targeted: workers at the bottom of the pay scale get a legally guaranteed raise, and the groups historically paid least under the law — tipped workers and people with disabilities in sheltered workshops — are brought onto the standard wage. The real costs are higher labor costs for low-wage employers and some risk of reduced hiring at the margin, and the bill phases both the wage floor and the exceptions in over six years, which softens the shock but also delays the benefit. A fair reading is that the gains for low-wage workers outweigh the adjustment costs, but the bill makes no concessions to employers or to the argument that local costs vary, which is part of why it drew no Republican support.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representatives Bobby Scott, the top Democrat on the Education and the Workforce Committee, and 172 other House Democrats introduced the bill on July 25, 2023, and it was referred to that committee the same day.
The House action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-wage employers, particularly in the restaurant industry, are better off because the bill never advanced: the federal minimum stays at $7.25, the $2.13 tipped cash wage stays in place, and the subminimum wage for workers with disabilities continues. The bill's 172 House Democratic supporters had no Republican counterpart willing to move it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers of minimum-wage and tipped workers

sides.party_line_note: All 172 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it, and a Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would phase out the tipped-employee cash wage exception, requiring restaurants eventually to pay servers the full minimum wage on top of letting them keep tips. Restaurant industry interest in keeping the current two-tier tipped wage runs directly against the bill's benefit to tipped workers, who in many states can legally be paid $2.13 an hour in cash.

A phased rise to a $17 federal minimum raises payroll costs for businesses that rely on minimum-wage labor. Their preference for the $7.25 status quo is the reason the bill's main benefit — higher pay for their own workers — never happened.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and employers holding 14(c) special certificates
industries.note: The bill would bar new subminimum-wage certificates for workers with disabilities and sunset the program entirely. These employers' interest in keeping a legal subminimum wage runs against both the workers it applies to and the bill's public goal of competitive integrated employment.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker advocacy groups
industries.note: A higher, indexed minimum wage is a long-standing priority of these groups, and it lifts the floor for both their members and non-union low-wage workers.
